subChunks.title: String Basics & Immutability
subChunks.hookHtml: You have used String since day one — but String is not a primitive like int. It is an object, and that distinction has important consequences for how it behaves.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
String as an Object

A String is an instance of the java.lang.String class. Because it is an object, it has methods you can call on it.

String name = "Arcane Academy";
System.out.println(name.length());     // 14
System.out.println(name.charAt(7));    // A
System.out.println(name.isEmpty());    // false

Immutability

Strings are immutable — once created, they cannot be changed. Any operation that appears to modify a String actually creates a brand-new String object:

String s = "hello";
s = s.toUpperCase(); // creates a NEW String "HELLO"
// The original "hello" object is unchanged

String literal pool — string literals are cached in a special pool. Two variables assigned the same literal may point to the same object in memory.

Key methods at a glance:

  • length() — number of characters
  • charAt(i) — character at index i (0-based)
  • isEmpty() — true if length is 0

storyBeats.text: Archmage Eldrin leads the apprentice to a wall of stone tablets, each engraved with runes.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Observe these tablets. Once the runes are carved into the stone, they cannot be altered — the stone is immutable. If I wish to change the inscription, I must carve a new tablet. The original remains in the vault, unchanged.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: This is precisely how Java Strings work. Every 'modification' creates a fresh tablet. But you can always read from a tablet — asking its length, or the rune at a given position.

storyBeats.speaker: Reading a String
storyBeats.text:
String name = "Arcane Academy";
System.out.println(name.length());   // 14
System.out.println(name.charAt(7));  // A
System.out.println(name.isEmpty());  // false

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Remember: indices start at zero. The 'A' in 'Academy' sits at position 7, not 8. A common mistake costs many apprentices dearly!

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Given the string "Arcane Academy", print three things on separate lines:

  1. Its length
  2. The character at index 7
  3. Whether it is empty
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain String immutability in Java: what it means, why it matters, and what actually happens when you 'change' a String.

questions.explanationHtml: String indices are 0-based. Index 0 is 'H', index 1 is 'e'.

questions.questionHtml: Calling toUpperCase() on a String changes the original String object.
questions.explanationHtml: Strings are immutable. toUpperCase() returns a new String. The original is unchanged. You must assign the result: s = s.toUpperCase();.

questions.questionHtml: Why is String immutability considered a design advantage?
options: It makes Strings faster to create
It enables safe sharing and caching of String objects
It prevents Strings from being stored in variables
It forces all Strings to be uppercase
questions.correctAnswer: It enables safe sharing and caching of String objects
questions.explanationHtml: Because Strings cannot change, they can be safely shared between multiple variables and threads without risk of one part of the code unexpectedly modifying a value another part depends on. This enables the string literal pool.

subChunks.title: String Methods
subChunks.hookHtml: Java's String class comes with dozens of built-in methods — spells for slicing, searching, trimming, and transforming text without writing any extra logic yourself.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Essential String Methods

All of these methods return a new String (remember: immutability).

String s = "  Hello, World!  ";

s.toUpperCase()          // "  HELLO, WORLD!  "
s.toLowerCase()          // "  hello, world!  "
s.trim()                 // "Hello, World!" (removes leading/trailing spaces)
s.trim().substring(0,5)  // "Hello" (chars from index 0 up to but not including 5)
s.indexOf("World")       // 9 (position of first match, or -1 if not found)
s.contains("World")      // true
s.replace("World","Java") // "  Hello, Java!  "
s.split(", ")            // ["  Hello", "World!  "] array of parts

substring(start, end) — note that end is exclusive: "Hello".substring(1, 3) returns "el".

indexOf returns the starting index of the first occurrence, or -1 if not found.

storyBeats.text: Archmage Eldrin spreads a dusty prophecy scroll on the table. It is smudged, oddly capitalised, and needs work before the apprentice can read it.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: This scroll has come from a far archive — dusty, misaligned, in all the wrong cases. String methods are my toolkit for transforming such a raw text into something usable.

storyBeats.speaker: Transforming the prophecy
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: trim() removes the leading and trailing dust — spaces. toUpperCase() shouts the prophecy loudly. substring(4, 20) extracts exactly the key phrase we need. Each method returns a new scroll — the original is preserved in the vault!

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Given String spell = " fireball of doom ", print three things:

  1. The trimmed version (no leading/trailing spaces)
  2. The trimmed version in uppercase
  3. The first 8 characters of the trimmed version (should be fireball)

guidedPracticeTests.label: trim, toUpperCase, substring
guidedPracticeTests.expected:
fireball of doom
FIREBALL OF DOOM
fireball

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Describe at least five String methods, what they do, and give a small example of each.

questions.explanationHtml: trim() removes all leading and trailing whitespace characters, returning "hello".
substring(0,3) returns characters at indices 0, 1, 2 → "Arc". indexOf("c") finds 'c' at index 2.
indexOf returns -1 when the specified substring or character is not found.

questions.questionHtml: You want to check if a string ends with ".java". Which method is most appropriate?
questions.explanationHtml: endsWith(String suffix) returns true if the string ends with the given suffix. While contains or indexOf could work, endsWith is more expressive and correct.

subChunks.title: String Comparison & Formatting
subChunks.hookHtml: Why does "hello" == "hello" sometimes give unexpected results — and how do you produce beautifully formatted output like "The score is 95.00"?
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Comparing Strings: .equals() vs ==

The == operator compares references — whether two variables point to the exact same object in memory. Always use .equals() to compare String contents:

String a = new String("hello");
String b = new String("hello");
System.out.println(a == b);         // false — different objects!
System.out.println(a.equals(b));    // true  — same contents

equalsIgnoreCase() — compares without case sensitivity:

"Wizard".equalsIgnoreCase("wizard"); // true

String Formatting

String.format() and System.out.printf() use format specifiers:

  • %s — String
  • %d — integer
  • %f — floating point
  • %.2f — floating point with 2 decimal places
String msg = String.format("The %s ranks as level %d", "Apprentice", 3);
System.out.println(msg); // The Apprentice ranks as level 3

storyBeats.text: Archmage Eldrin holds two identical-looking scrolls, one in each hand. The apprentice squints — they look exactly alike.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: These two scrolls contain the same prophecy, word for word. Yet they are stored in different vaults — different locations in the archive. If you ask the librarian '==' — 'are these the exact same physical scroll?' — she says no. But if you ask '.equals()' — 'do they say the same thing?' — she says yes!

storyBeats.speaker: == vs .equals()
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: And when formatting proclamations, use String.format() — it lets you slot values into a template with precision. Perfect for tournament announcements!

storyBeats.speaker: Formatted proclamation
storyBeats.text:
String.format("The %s ranks as level %d", "Apprentice", 3);
// → "The Apprentice ranks as level 3"

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Given String a = "Wizard" and String b = "wizard", print three things:

  1. Whether a.equals(b) (true/false)
  2. Whether a.equalsIgnoreCase(b) (true/false)
  3. The result of String.format("The %s ranks as level %d", "Apprentice", 3)

guidedPracticeTests.label: equals, equalsIgnoreCase, format
guidedPracticeTests.expected:
false
true
The Apprentice ranks as level 3

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain why you should always use .equals() instead of == for String comparison in Java, and describe how String.format() works.

questions.questionHtml: Which method compares the contents of two Strings in Java?
questions.explanationHtml: .equals() compares the actual character sequence. == compares object references (memory addresses), not contents.
%d formats the integer 95, %.1f formats 100.0 with one decimal place.
equalsIgnoreCase ignores case differences when comparing. "hello" and "HELLO" have the same letters, so it returns true.

questions.questionHtml: A user types a password at runtime (not a literal). Which comparison is correct?
questions.explanationHtml: Runtime Strings are not guaranteed to share memory, so == will give wrong results. Always use .equals() to compare String contents reliably.

subChunks.title: StringBuilder
subChunks.hookHtml: If you concatenate Strings inside a loop using +, Java creates a brand-new String object on every iteration. Concatenating 1,000 strings produces 999 throwaway objects. StringBuilder solves this with a single mutable buffer.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
StringBuilder: The Efficient Scroll

StringBuilder is a mutable sequence of characters. Unlike String, it can be modified in place without creating new objects.

StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
sb.append("Hello");
sb.append(", ");
sb.append("World");
System.out.println(sb.toString()); // Hello, World

Key methods:

  • append(x) — adds x to the end
  • insert(index, x) — inserts x at the given position
  • delete(start, end) — removes characters from start to end-1
  • reverse() — reverses the contents
  • toString() — converts to a regular String

Why it matters in loops:

// Bad — creates a new String each iteration:
String result = "";
for (int i = 1; i <= 1000; i++) {
    result += i; // 999 garbage String objects!
}

// Good — one mutable buffer:
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
for (int i = 1; i <= 1000; i++) {
    sb.append(i);
}
String result = sb.toString();

storyBeats.text: Archmage Eldrin faces an enormous wall scroll. A novice apprentice is painstakingly rewriting the entire scroll from scratch each time he needs to add a single sentence.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Stop! Every time you add a sentence, you copy every word that came before it onto a new scroll — then discard the old one. By the time you have written the prophecy's hundredth sentence, you have filled the vault with ninety-nine useless scrolls.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Instead, use a living scroll — a StringBuilder. Append each sentence directly to the same surface. Only at the end do you seal it into a permanent, immutable String.

storyBeats.speaker: Building a prophecy efficiently
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: One scroll, three sentences appended directly. No waste. Call toString() at the very end when you need the sealed, immutable result.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Use a StringBuilder to build a comma-separated list of numbers 1 through 5: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Print the final result.

Hint: append each number, and for numbers 1–4 also append ", ". For the last number (5), do not append a trailing comma.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain why StringBuilder is more efficient than using + for String concatenation inside a loop, and describe three useful StringBuilder methods.

questions.questionHtml: Which method converts a StringBuilder to a regular String?
questions.explanationHtml: sb.toString() returns the current contents of the StringBuilder as an immutable String.

questions.questionHtml: StringBuilder objects are mutable — you can change their contents after creation.
questions.explanationHtml: That is the key difference from String. StringBuilder maintains a resizable internal buffer that can be modified with append, insert, delete, etc.
reverse() reverses the character sequence in place. "Hello" reversed is "olleH".

questions.questionHtml: In which situation is it MOST important to use StringBuilder instead of String concatenation?
options: Joining two strings once outside a loop
Concatenating strings inside a loop that runs thousands of times
questions.correctAnswer: Concatenating strings inside a loop that runs thousands of times
questions.explanationHtml: String + in a loop creates a new object every iteration. For small or one-off concatenations, + is fine. For loops, use StringBuilder to avoid creating thousands of intermediate objects.
